summary: Specifies iSCSI, which carries SCSI storage commands over TCP so computers can use disks and tapes across an IP network. It follows the standard SCSI architecture model and maps SCSI request and response exchanges onto TCP connections. It was updated by RFC 3980, RFC 4850, RFC 5048 and RFC 7146, and replaced by RFC 7143.

eli5.summary: Normally a disk plugs right into a computer. iSCSI lets a computer use a disk somewhere else on the network as if it were plugged in, by sending the disk commands through the network.

questions: how does iscsi work over tcp
what is an iscsi initiator and target
subtitle: How SCSI storage commands travel over ordinary TCP connections, so a computer can use disks on the network as if they were local.

tldr.problem: SCSI, the family of protocols computers use to talk to disks and tapes, had only been mapped onto special I/O interconnects with limited distance. IP networks had become fast enough to carry it, but a mapping onto TCP was needed.
tldr.mechanism: iSCSI wraps SCSI commands, data and status in iSCSI Protocol Data Units (PDUs) sent over one or more TCP connections that together form a session. A login phase authenticates the parties and negotiates parameters, and numbering schemes keep commands ordered and recoverable.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3720 was a Proposed Standard, was updated by RFC 3980, RFC 4850, RFC 5048 and RFC 7146, and has been obsoleted by RFC 7143, which is now the iSCSI specification.

facts.label: Default TCP port
facts.value: 3260 (860 is the system port, never the default)

today: RFC 3720 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 7143, which is where the current iSCSI specification lives. It was also updated by RFC 3980, RFC 4850, RFC 5048 and RFC 7146.

sections.title: Why SCSI Needed an IP Mapping
sections.content:
SCSI is a family of protocols for talking to I/O devices, especially storage. It is a client-server design: clients are called initiators, and they send commands to logical units that live inside a server called a target. A SCSI transport maps this client-server protocol onto a particular interconnect.

SCSI had been mapped onto transports such as Parallel SCSI, IPI, IEEE-1394 (firewire) and Fibre Channel. The RFC notes that these are I/O specific and have limited distance capabilities. iSCSI instead carries SCSI over TCP/IP, which lets it use existing Internet infrastructure and management facilities and removes the distance limit.

The goal is to be fully compliant with the standardized SCSI architecture model. Each SCSI command has an optional data phase (a WRITE sends data to the target, a READ brings data back) and a required response phase in which the target returns the final status.
sections.eli5: A computer can already ask a disk next to it to read or write. iSCSI lets it ask a disk far away instead, by mailing the same requests over the internet's normal delivery service, TCP.

sections.title: Initiators, Targets and Sessions
sections.content:
An iSCSI session is a group of one or more TCP connections between an initiator and a target. It is loosely equivalent to a SCSI I_T nexus. Connections can be added to and removed from a session, and each one is identified by a connection ID (CID). Across all connections, the initiator sees one target image, so identifiers such as the LUN are the same everywhere. Implementations MUST support at least one TCP connection per session and MAY support several.

Everything is carried in iSCSI PDUs. Two ideas keep this orderly. First, connection allegiance: the response and any related data for a request MUST travel over the same connection as the request, unless the task is explicitly reassigned after a failure. Second, an initiator and target can interleave unrelated commands, data and responses over the session.

The mapping model distinguishes a Network Entity (a device or gateway reachable from the IP network), iSCSI Nodes (single initiators or targets) and Network Portals (an IP address and TCP port pair). A target listens on a TCP port, and the RFC's diagram shows TCP port 3260. A discovery session is a second session type that accepts only a text request with the SendTargets key and a logout request with the reason close the session.
sections.eli5: A session is like a phone call between you and the disk that can use several phone lines at once. All the lines belong to the same call, but each question and its answer have to stay on the same line.

sections.title: iSCSI Names
sections.content:
Every iSCSI node, initiator or target, MUST have an iSCSI name. Names are globally unique and permanent, they do not imply a location or address, and they do not rely on a central name broker. A name belongs to the logical iSCSI node, not to a network card, so replacing a NIC does not require reconfiguring storage allocations. Implementations MUST accept names up to 223 bytes. A name is a UTF-8 string in Normalization Form C that passes the iSCSI stringprep template.

Two type designators are defined. The iqn. form is built from a date code in yyyy-mm format, the reversed domain name of the naming authority, and an optional colon-prefixed string chosen by the domain owner. The date records a month in which the authority owned the domain. The eui. form is followed by an IEEE EUI-64 identifier written as 16 hexadecimal digits.

The RFC's examples are iqn.2001-04.com.example:storage:diskarrays-sn-a8675309 and eui.02004567A425678D. An initiator can find the target names it may use, with their addresses, through the SendTargets text request or the other techniques in RFC 3721.
sections.eli5: An iSCSI name is like a person's full name rather than their street address. If the person moves house, the name stays the same, so everyone still knows who they mean.

sections.title: Login and Parameter Negotiation
sections.content:
Before any SCSI command can be sent, each TCP connection goes through a Login Phase. Its purposes are to enable the connection for iSCSI, authenticate the parties, negotiate session parameters and mark the connection as belonging to a session. Only Login Request and Login Response PDUs are allowed until it ends. The initial request MUST carry the InitiatorName key, and for a normal session also TargetName. Once login succeeds, the session enters the Full Feature Phase and SCSI commands may flow.

Login has two optional stages, security negotiation and operational parameter negotiation, and at least one must be present. The T (transit) bit and the CSG and NSG fields move the connection from one stage to the next. The target decides whether the login creates a new session, adds a connection or reinstates one based on the ISID, the TSIH (zero for a new session) and the CID.

Parameters are exchanged as key=value text in UTF-8, each pair ended by a null byte. A key is either declared by one side or negotiated: the proposer sends a value or a list in order of preference and the acceptor answers with its choice, or with Reject, Irrelevant or NotUnderstood. The same mechanism is used in the Full Feature Phase through Text requests. New private keys start with X- and a reversed domain name, and registered ones start with X#.

Several key defaults matter for data transfer. InitialR2T defaults to Yes and ImmediateData to Yes, MaxRecvDataSegmentLength defaults to 8192 bytes, MaxBurstLength to 262144 and FirstBurstLength to 65536. MaxConnections defaults to 1 and ErrorRecoveryLevel to 0. The HeaderDigest and DataDigest keys default to None, and the digest that every implementation MUST support is CRC32C.
sections.eli5: Login is the polite hello before a conversation. The two sides show who they are, then agree on the rules, such as how big each package can be, before they start sending real work.

sections.title: Commands, Data and Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
A SCSI command travels in a SCSI Command PDU and the target answers with a SCSI Response PDU carrying the status. Data moves in Data-Out PDUs (initiator to target, for writes) and Data-In PDUs (target to initiator, for reads). For a write, the target uses Ready To Transfer (R2T) PDUs to ask the initiator for the next chunk. The initiator may also send unsolicited data, either as immediate data inside the command PDU or as separate Data-Out PDUs, up to FirstBurstLength; everything after that MUST be solicited by R2T. Phase collapse lets a command and its data, or data and status, share one PDU.

Three numbering schemes keep this ordered. CmdSN numbers commands across the whole session using a 32-bit counter, and the target delivers them for execution in that order. The target advertises a window with ExpCmdSN (the next command it expects) and MaxCmdSN (the highest it will accept), which doubles as flow control. StatSN numbers responses per connection and the initiator acknowledges it with ExpStatSN. DataSN and R2TSN number data and R2T PDUs within a command so that missing ones are detectable.

Control operations also use PDUs. A Task Management request can abort a task, abort or clear a task set, reset a logical unit or target, or reassign a task to another connection. A NOP-Out and NOP-In pair works as a ping and can carry sequence numbers when traffic is one-way. A Reject PDU reports an iSCSI error, and the Asynchronous Message PDU carries events from the target.
sections.eli5: Every request gets a number, like a ticket at a deli counter, so orders are handled in the right order. When you want to hand over a big box, the shop first says it is ready, then you send the box in pieces.

sections.title: The PDU Format
sections.content:
Every iSCSI PDU starts with a fixed 48-byte Basic Header Segment (BHS). It can be followed by Additional Header Segments, an optional header digest, an optional data segment and an optional data digest. All segments are padded to a multiple of four bytes, and multi-byte integers use network byte order.

The BHS always has the Opcode and DataSegmentLength in the same place, and the Initiator Task Tag and the 64-bit LUN field are placed consistently across PDU types. The I bit marks a request for immediate delivery, and the F bit marks the final PDU of a sequence. Initiators MUST NOT use target opcodes, and targets MUST NOT use initiator opcodes.

The optional header digest and data digest are negotiated at login. They are separate so that a router that forwards a message and changes only the header need only recompute the header digest. The Extended CDB and the bidirectional expected read-data length can be carried in Additional Header Segments.

The SCSI Command PDU adds its own fields after the common header: an Expected Data Transfer Length, the CmdSN, the ExpStatSN and a 16-byte area for the SCSI Command Descriptor Block. The R and W flag bits say whether the command reads or writes data, and its task attribute can be untagged, simple, ordered, head of queue or ACA.
sections.eli5: Every message starts with the same kind of address label, always the same size and always in the same layout. That way the receiver can read the label quickly and know what kind of message is inside.

sections.title: Error Handling and Recovery
sections.content:
Two situations drove the recovery design. A PDU can fail its digest check and be dropped even though TCP delivered it, and a TCP connection can fail at any moment while tasks are active. iSCSI therefore defines four classes of recovery: within a command, within a connection, connection recovery and session recovery. Implementations choose how much of this to support.

The support level is negotiated with ErrorRecoveryLevel, and the lower of the two values becomes the operational level. Implementations MUST support level 0; levels 1 and 2 are optional.

The mechanisms include the SNACK request, which asks the target to resend status, data or R2T PDUs, the recovery R2T, command retry, NOP probes of the other side's sequence numbers, and the Task Reassign function, which moves a task's connection allegiance after a failure. After a TCP connection failure the initiator MUST close the connection, log it out for recovery and reassign its commands. Session recovery is the fallback when everything else has failed: all connections are closed and the session restarts from login.
sections.eli5: If a letter gets lost or smudged, you can ask for another copy. If a whole mail route breaks, you switch to another route. If everything is broken, you hang up and start the call again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Storage used to sit on directly attached or separate networks, but running SCSI over IP means security must be addressed. Implementations MUST provide protection against active and passive attacks, and the RFC says iSCSI SHOULD NOT be configured without security except in closed environments with no security risk. Details of the threats and mechanisms are in RFC 3723.

Two mechanisms complement each other. In-band authentication happens during login on every new connection and gives end-to-end trust at login time. IPsec protects packets between the IP endpoints. After login, if IPsec is not used, all PDUs travel in clear. The authentication methods named in the text are Kerberos, SPKM, SRP and CHAP, and a method that sends clear text passwords is not acceptable.

All compliant implementations MUST implement CHAP (RFC 1994) including target authentication. They MUST support random CHAP secrets of up to 128 bits. A secret shorter than 96 random bits requires IPsec encryption, and the same secret MUST NOT be used for authenticating both initiators and targets, which prevents a reflection attack. For IPsec, ESP in tunnel mode MUST be implemented, with HMAC-SHA1 for integrity and 3DES in CBC mode for confidentiality, and IKE with pre-shared keys MUST be supported.
sections.eli5: Because the disk is reached over a shared network, anyone could try to pretend to be you. Login makes both sides prove who they are, and an extra locked tunnel can hide what is being sent.

messages.note: The target receives the command and queues it.

messages.note: Ready to process the WRITE command.

messages.note: Repeated for each piece of data.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: Immediate delivery marker on request PDUs.

fields.name: Opcode
fields.desc: Type of iSCSI PDU the header carries.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Final (or only) PDU of a sequence.

fields.name: TotalAHSLength
fields.desc: Length of all AHS segments in four-byte words.

fields.name: DataSegmentLength
fields.desc: Data segment length in bytes, excluding padding.

fields.name: LUN or Opcode-specific
fields.desc: 64-bit logical unit number, formatted per SAM-2.

fields.name: Initiator Task Tag
fields.desc: Uniquely identifies the task session-wide while it exists.

fields.name: Opcode-specific
fields.desc: Remaining header bytes, used differently by each PDU type.

items.label: SCSI Command
items.desc: Encapsulates a SCSI Command Descriptor Block.

items.label: Logout Request
items.desc: Orderly close of a connection or session.

items.label: SCSI Response
items.desc: SCSI status and possibly sense information.

items.label: Task Management Response
items.desc: Answer to a task management function.

items.label: R2T
items.desc: Sent by the target when it is ready to receive data.

items.label: Asynchronous Message
items.desc: Special conditions announced by the target.
